title: Age after age
hookLine: Arjuna asks how Krishna can be so old, and Krishna tells why God keeps coming
carry: whenever dharma slips, god comes again
tomorrow: a hunter's arrow hits Krishna. what does Krishna say to him?
last: BUT GOD COMES SMALL ENOUGH TO HOLD IS THE LORD HIMSELF.

lines: A SOUND THAT MEANS IT'S STARTING.
HOW CAN YOU BE THAT OLD?
cards: Some sounds mean it's starting before anyone says a word: the whistle before a game, the first chord at a concert, the kettle about to boil. In the Bhagavad Gita it's conch shells.
Two armies face each other, and the conches are blown, one after another, until the noise makes the earth and sky ring.

Between the armies, the warrior Arjuna puts down his bow, and his charioteer, Krishna, starts to teach. Partway through, Krishna says he gave this teaching to the sun god long ago. Arjuna asks the obvious thing.
How? You were born recently. The sun god came first.

teach.b: This is the fourth chapter of the Gita, and Krishna answers in layers. First: you and I have both been born many times, Arjuna. I remember them all; you don't.
Then something stranger. I am unborn and undying, the Lord of all beings, and still, through my own power, I come into being.
Unborn, and born anyway. Then the two verses that sound like the whole series of descents explaining itself.

Whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, Krishna says, I send myself forth. To protect the good, to undo those who do harm, and to set dharma firmly in place again, I come into being age after age.
In Sanskrit, that last phrase is sambhavami yuge yuge. Listen to it: yuge yuge, age, age. The word repeats the way the coming repeats.
So the answer to Arjuna isn't a birthday. It's a rhythm: when the world tips over, he comes, and he has come before.
This is the heart of what Hindus mean by an avatar, avatara in Sanskrit: a descent, God crossing down into the world. The fish in the flood.
The boar lifting the earth from the waters. The man-lion at the doorway. The dwarf and his three steps.
Each arrives when dharma has slipped, and the Gita names the rhythm in the voice of the one who keeps arriving.

how: In some Hindu homes and temples a conch is blown at the start of worship, and Gita 4.7–8 is among the verses some Hindus learn by heart.

o: the warrior who put down his bow in the chariot
the charioteer who says he comes age after age
the sun god who first heard the old teaching

games.q: Krishna's answer, in layers — tap the pairs.
p: I remember them all; you don't
and still I come into being

s: in the Gita, Krishna says he has been born only once
he tells Arjuna they've both been born many times, and only he remembers.
yuge yuge means age after age
sambhavami yuge yuge: I come into being, age after age.
the Gita's teaching begins in a temple
it begins in a chariot between two armies, after the conches sound.

games.q: Arjuna's puzzle: Krishna was born recently, so how could he have taught the sun god long ago? what's Krishna's answer?
o: he is unborn and undying, yet comes into being by his own power, again and again.
the sun god was actually younger than Krishna all along.
he only meant it as a figure of speech, nothing more.
games.why: Gita 4.5–6: we've both been born many times, and I remember them all. unborn, yet I come into being: that's the avatar.

practice: Many Hindus learn these two verses by heart. If you'd like, say yuge yuge softly on each breath out: age, age.

If Sanskrit isn't part of your practice, choose one sound that keeps coming back where you are, a clock, a fan, your own breath, and hear each return as if it were the first. When your mind drifts, the next return is your way back.

wordCard.voice: Krishna: the charioteer of the Gita, who says that whenever dharma slips, he comes, age after age: the avatar's own account of itself.

carryVoice: For the road: whenever dharma slips, God comes again, yuge yuge, age after age. Until tomorrow.
